info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Abstract:
This paper introduces the Generality-Accuracy-Simplicity (GAS) framework to analyze how large language models (LLMs) are reshaping organizations and competitive strategy. We argue that viewing AI as a simple reduction in input costs overlooks two critical dynamics: (a) the inherent trade-offs among generality, accuracy, and simplicity, and (b) the redistribution of complexity across stakeholders. While LLMs appear to defy the traditional trade-off by offering high generality and accuracy through simple interfaces, this user-facing simplicity masks a significant shift of complexity to infrastructure, compliance, and specialized personnel. The GAS trade-off, therefore, does not disappear but is relocated from the user to the organization, creating new managerial challenges, particularly around accuracy in high-stakes applications. We contend that competitive advantage no longer stems from mere AI adoption, but from mastering this redistributed complexity through the design of abstraction layers, workflow alignment, and complementary expertise. This study advances AI strategy by clarifying how scalable cognition relocates complexity and redefines the conditions for technology integration.

Abstract:
The rapid proliferation of generative AI has raised questions about the competitiveness of lower-parameter, locally tunable, open-weight models relative to high-parameter, API-guarded, closed-weight models in terms of performance, domain adaptation, cost, and generalization. Centering under-resourced yet risk-intolerant settings in government, research, and healthcare, we see for-profit closed-weight models as incompatible with requirements for transparency, privacy, adaptability, and standards of evidence. Yet the performance penalty in using open-weight models, especially in low-data and low-resource settings, is unclear. We assess the feasibility of using smaller, open-weight models to replace GPT-4-Turbo in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned regimes, assuming access to only a single, low-cost GPU. We assess value-sensitive issues around bias, privacy, and abstention on three additional tasks relevant to those topics. We find that with relatively low effort, very low absolute monetary cost, and relatively little data for fine-tuning, small open-weight models can achieve competitive performance in domain-adapted tasks without sacrificing generality. We then run experiments considering practical issues in bias, privacy, and hallucination risk, finding that open models offer several benefits over closed models. We intend this work as a case study in understanding the opportunity cost of reproducibility and transparency over for-profit state-of-the-art zero shot performance, finding this cost to be marginal under realistic settings.

Abstract:
As the open-weight AI landscape continues to proliferate-with model development, significant investment, and user interest-it becomes increasingly important to predict which models will ultimately drive innovation and shape AI ecosystems. Building on parallels with citation dynamics in scientific literature, we propose a framework to quantify how an open-weight model's influence evolves. Specifically, we adapt the model introduced by Wang et al. for scientific citations, using three key parameters-immediacy, longevity, and relative fitness-to track the cumulative number of fine-tuned models of an open-weight model. Our findings reveal that this citation-style approach can effectively capture the diverse trajectories of open-weight model adoption, with most models fitting well and outliers indicating unique patterns or abrupt jumps in usage.

Abstract:
Foundation models are powerful technologies: how they are released publicly directly shapes their societal impact. In this position paper, we focus on open foundation models, defined here as those with broadly available model weights (e.g. Llama 2, Stable Diffusion XL). We identify five distinctive properties (e.g. greater customizability, poor monitoring) of open foundation models that lead to both their benefits and risks. Open foundation models present significant benefits, with some caveats, that span innovation, competition, the distribution of decision-making power, and transparency. To understand their risks of misuse, we design a risk assessment framework for analyzing their marginal risk. Across several misuse vectors (e.g. cyberattacks, bioweapons), we find that current research is insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies. The framework helps explain why the marginal risk is low in some cases, clarifies disagreements about misuse risks by revealing that past work has focused on different subsets of the framework with different assumptions, and articulates a way forward for more constructive debate. Overall, our work helps support a more grounded assessment of the societal impact of open foundation models by outlining what research is needed to empirically validate their theoretical benefits and risks.

Abstract:
Welcome to the eighth edition of the AI Index report. The 2025 Index is our most comprehensive to date and arrives at an important moment, as AI's influence across society, the economy, and global governance continues to intensify. New in this year's report are in-depth analyses of the evolving landscape of AI hardware, novel estimates of inference costs, and new analyses of AI publication and patenting trends. We also introduce fresh data on corporate adoption of responsible AI practices, along with expanded coverage of AI's growing role in science and medicine. Since its founding in 2017 as an offshoot of the One Hundred Year Study of Artificial Intelligence, the AI Index has been committed to equipping policymakers, journalists, executives, researchers, and the public with accurate, rigorously validated, and globally sourced data. Our mission has always been to help these stakeholders make better-informed decisions about the development and deployment of AI. In a world where AI is discussed everywhere - from boardrooms to kitchen tables - this mission has never been more essential. The AI Index continues to lead in tracking and interpreting the most critical trends shaping the field - from the shifting geopolitical landscape and the rapid evolution of underlying technologies, to AI's expanding role in business, policymaking, and public life. Longitudinal tracking remains at the heart of our mission. In a domain advancing at breakneck speed, the Index provides essential context - helping us understand where AI stands today, how it got here, and where it may be headed next. Recognized globally as one of the most authoritative resources on artificial intelligence, the AI Index has been cited in major media outlets such as The New York Times, Bloomberg, and The Guardian; referenced in hundreds of academic papers; and used by policymakers and government agencies around the world.

Abstract:
AI research is increasingly industry-driven, making it crucial to understand company contributions to this field. We compare leading AI companies by research publications, citations, size of training runs, and contributions to algorithmic innovations. Our analysis reveals the substantial role played by Google, OpenAI and Meta. We find that these three companies have been responsible for some of the largest training runs, developed a large fraction of the algorithmic innovations that underpin large language models, and led in various metrics of citation impact. In contrast, leading Chinese companies such as Tencent and Baidu had a lower impact on many of these metrics compared to US counterparts. We observe many industry labs are pursuing large training runs, and that training runs from relative newcomers -- such as OpenAI and Anthropic -- have matched or surpassed those of long-standing incumbents such as Google. The data reveals a diverse ecosystem of companies steering AI progress, though US labs such as Google, OpenAI and Meta lead across critical metrics.

less open-weight use, consistent with greater reliance on
closed models. Second, industry involvement is associated
with model extension, suggesting that corporate resources
reach science through coauthorship, though this channel is
concentrated in Computer Science and Global North collaborations. Third, the gap across research systems is not
one of AI adoption but of control. Off-the-shelf use is rising across fields and country groups, and the least publicly
funded group, the Global South, now has the highest share
of API-only engagement (0.4% to 10.0% of engaged papers).
China shows the opposite profile: the highest public-funding
share and lowest API-only engagement, with extension remaining stable as it declines across the Global North. Standard capacity indicators show convergence in AI adoption
even as dependence on proprietary infrastructure diverges</jats:p>

Abstract:
<title>Abstract</title>
                <p>National strategies for artificial intelligence (AI) are usually compared by the resources they mobilise: researchers, research budgets, private investment and computing infrastructure. Far less is known about how efficiently those resources are converted into AI capability, and why conversion differs among countries with comparable endowments. This article operationalises a three-layer view of national AI capability (invention, industrialisation and operationalisation) and measures conversion ratios for China, Japan and South Korea between 2017 and 2025, using the United States as the frontier reference. The analysis combines model-level data from Epoch AI, bibliometric data from OpenAlex, input indicators from the World Bank, investment, patent and diffusion data from the Stanford AI Index 2026, and pillar scores from the Government AI Readiness Index 2025. Three findings stand out. First, Japan is the lowest-converting case in almost every link: it produced 52 AI models in nine years against 87 for South Korea, despite larger research, R&D and compute endowments, and its compute-weighted conversion is an order of magnitude below that of its neighbours. Second, the Japanese gap lies in the knowledge-to-model and compute-to-model links, not in the capital link. Third, conversion aligns more closely with the state's policy capacity than with infrastructure or sector maturity: Japan and South Korea score almost identically on development and diffusion, but 70 versus 96 on policy capacity. The results are robust to fractional counting and compute weighting. The article argues that AI sovereignty is a problem of governing conversion, not only of accumulating inputs.</p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities on national competitiveness through a comparative analysis of the IMD World Competitiveness Index and three major AI indices: Oxford AI Readiness, Tortoise AI Index and Stanford AI Index. For Least Developed Countries (LDCs), a 2 × 2 strategy matrix outlines low‐cost, high‐impact AI initiatives to enable a bypass strategy, leveraging open innovation ecosystems to circumvent traditional industrial pathways. Findings underscore AI's transformative role in redefining competitiveness, driven by qualitative capabilities like efficiency, innovation and governance, offering actionable pathways for advanced economies and LDCs to close competitiveness gaps through strategic AI integration and DPI investments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Foundation model developers are among the world’s most important companies. As these companies become increasingly consequential, how do their transparency practices evolve? The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index is the third edition of an annual effort to characterize and quantify the transparency of foundation model developers. The 2025 FMTI introduces new indicators related to data acquisition, usage data, and monitoring and evaluates companies like Alibaba, DeepSeek, and xAI for the first time. The 2024 FMTI reported that transparency was improving, but the 2025 FMTI finds this progress has deteriorated: the average score out of 100 fell from 58 in 2024 to 40 in 2025. Companies are most opaque about their training data and training compute as well as the post-deployment usage and impact of their flagship models. While companies tend to disclose evaluations of model capabilities and risks, limited methodological transparency, third-party involvement, reproducibility, and reporting of train-test overlap pose challenges. In spite of this general trend, IBM stands out as a positive outlier, scoring 95, in contrast to the lowest scorers, xAI and Midjourney, at just 14. Several groups of companies score higher than the mean: open model developers, enterprise-focused B2B companies, companies that prepare their own transparency reports, and signatories to the EU AI Act General Purpose-AI Code of Practice. The five members of the Frontier Model Forum we score end up in the middle of the Index: we posit that major companies aim to avoid particularly low rankings but also lack incentives to be highly transparent. As policymakers around the world increasingly mandate certain types of transparency, this work reveals the current state of transparency for foundation model developers, how it may change given newly enacted policy, and where more aggressive policy interventions are necessary to address critical information deficits.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study addresses critical questions about how current evaluative frameworks for academic research can effectively translate scholarly findings into practical applications and policies to tackle societal ‘grand challenges’. This scoping review analysis was conducted using bibliometric methods and AI tools. Articles were drawn from a wide range of disciplines, with particular emphasis on the business and management fields, focusing on the burgeoning scholarship area of ‘business as a force for good’. The novel integration of generative AI research approaches underscores the transformative potential of AI‐human collaboration in academic research. Metadata from 4051 articles were examined in the scoping review, with only 370 articles (9.1%) explicitly identified as relevant to societal impact. This finding reveals a substantial and concerning gap in research addressing the urgent social and environmental issues of our time. To address this gap, the study identifies six meta‐themes related to enhancing the societal impact of research: business applications; faculty publication pressure; societal impact focus; sustainable development; university and scholarly rankings; and reference to responsible research frameworks. Key findings highlight critical misalignments between research outputs and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and a lack of practical business applications of research insights. The results emphasise the urgent need for academic institutions to expand evaluation criteria beyond traditional metrics to prioritise real‐world impacts. Recommendations include developing holistic evaluation frameworks and incentivising research that addresses pressing societal challenges—shifting academia from a ‘scholar‐to‐scholar’ to a ‘scholar‐to‐society’ paradigm. The implications of this shift are applied to business‐related scholarship and its potential to inspire meaningful societal impact through business practice.

Abstract:
Many companies use large language models (LLMs) offered as a service, like OpenAl's GPT-4, to create AI-enabled product experiences. Along with the benefits of ease-of-use and shortened time-to-solution, this reliance on proprietary services has downsides in model control, performance reliability, uptime predictability, and cost. At the same time, a flurry of open-source small language models (SLMs) has been made avail-able for commercial use. However, their readiness to replace existing capabilities remains unclear, and a systematic approach to holistically evaluate these SLMs is not readily available. This paper presents a systematic evaluation methodology and a characterization of modern open-source SLMs and their trade-offs when replacing proprietary LLMs for a real-world product feature. We have designed SLaM, an open-source automated analysis tool that enables the quantitative and qualitative testing of product features utilizing arbitrary SLMs. Using SLaM, we examine the quality and performance characteristics of modern SLMs relative to an existing customer-facing implementation using the OpenAI GPT-4 API. Across 9 SLMs and their 29 variants, we observe that SLMs provide competitive results, significant performance consistency improvements, and a cost reduction of 5xrv29x when compared to GPT-4.

Abstract:
POKT Network's decentralized Remote Procedure Call (RPC) infrastructure, surpassing 740 billion requests since launching on MainNet in 2020, is well-positioned to extend into providing AI inference services with minimal design or implementation modifications. This litepaper illustrates how the network's open-source and permissionless design aligns incentives among model researchers, hardware operators, API providers and users whom we term model Sources, Suppliers, Gateways and Applications respectively. Through its Relay Mining algorithm, POKT creates a transparent marketplace where costs and earnings directly reflect cryptographically verified usage. This decentralized framework offers large model AI researchers a new avenue to disseminate their work and generate revenue without the complexities of maintaining infrastructure or building end-user products. Supply scales naturally with demand, as evidenced in recent years and the protocol's free market dynamics. POKT Gateways facilitate network growth, evolution, adoption, and quality by acting as application-facing load balancers, providing value-added features without managing LLM nodes directly. This vertically decoupled network, battle tested over several years, is set up to accelerate the adoption, operation, innovation and financialization of open-source models. It is the first mature permissionless network whose quality of service competes with centralized entities set up to provide application grade inference.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) require substantial computational resources, making efficient inference a critical challenge. As the demand for LLMs grows in serverless and large-scale deployments, scheduling techniques play a pivotal role in optimizing inference performance, balancing latency, cost, and throughput. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of scheduling strategies for LLM serving across both the control and data planes. We explore key challenges such as cold start latency, HOL blocking, resource utilization, and dynamic workload variations. We analyze scheduling techniques, including reinforcement learning-based workload management, adaptive batching, speculative execution, and multi-tenant scheduling. Additionally, we compare scheduling frameworks across latency reduction, cost efficiency, and scalability. Finally, we identify open research directions, including ML-driven adaptive scheduling, energy-aware inference, and heterogeneous hardware utilization. This survey aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners optimizing LLM inference at scale and is maintained as a live document, updated monthly to reflect ongoing developments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This paper studies incentives for openness in foundation models (FMs). Using data from Hugging Face with model documentations, we develop and estimate a two-stage dynamic structural model in which the FM owners choose the degree of openness for their models, and downstream AI developers decide which FM to adopt for application development. Our estimates indicate that the short-term benefits of openness account for less than half of its contemporaneous costs, implying that immediate returns alone cannot rationalize observed openness choices of FM owners. Instead, longer-term considerations play a central role. By increasing openness, owners gain knowledge spillovers from downstream developers, which expands later adoption by improving the quality of subsequent model generations. This intertemporal feedback mechanism raises long-term continuation value and helps explain why FM owners adopt open-source strategies despite limited short-run monetization benefits.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The world has recently witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in demands for Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence applications. This spike in demand has imposed tremendous strain on the underlying technology stack in supply chain, GPU-accelerated hardware, software, datacenter power density, and energy consumption. If left on the current technological trajectory, future demands show insurmountable spending trends, further limiting market players, stifling innovation, and widening the technology gap. To address these challenges, we propose a fundamental change in the AI training infrastructure throughout the technology ecosystem. The changes require advancements in supercomputing and novel AI training approaches, from high-end software to low-level hardware, microprocessor, and chip design, while advancing the energy efficiency required by a sustainable infrastructure. This paper presents the analytical framework that quantitatively highlights the challenges and points to the opportunities to reduce the barriers to entry for training large language models.

Abstract:
Drawing insights from the field of innovation economics, we discuss the likely competitive environment shaping generative AI advances. Central to our analysis are the concepts of appropriability —whether firms in the industry are able to control the knowledge generated by their innovations—and complementary assets —whether effective entry requires access to specialized infrastructure and capabilities to which incumbent firms can ration access. While the rapid improvements in AI foundation models promise transformative impacts across broad sectors of the economy, we argue that tight control over complementary assets will likely result in a concentrated market structure, as in past episodes of technological upheaval. We suggest the likely paths through which incumbent firms may restrict entry, confining newcomers to subordinate roles and stifling broad sectoral innovation. We conclude with speculations regarding how this oligopolistic future might be averted. Policy interventions aimed at fractionalizing or facilitating shared access to complementary assets might help preserve competition and incentives for extending the generative AI frontier. Ironically, the best hopes for a vibrant open source AI ecosystem might rest on the presence of a “rogue” technology giant, who might choose openness and engagement with smaller firms as a strategic weapon wielded against other incumbents.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The artificial intelligence industry exhibits a paradoxical market structure without precedent in the history of technology industries: extreme concentration at the infrastructure layer, where a handful of companies control frontier foundation model development due to capital requirements exceeding $100 million per training run, coexists with radical fragmentation at the application layer, where thousands of startups build products on top of these models through API access. This paper analyzes how this structural paradox reshapes industry value chains across sectors, applying Porter's value chain analysis and platform economics theory to what this paper terms the AI Value Stackthe layered architecture of compute, foundation models, middleware, applications, and distribution through which AI capabilities are created and commercialized. The paper introduces the AI Value Migration Model, which maps how value capture shifts across the stack depending on whether AI capabilities are commoditizing (inference costs declining, open-source models proliferating) or concentrating (proprietary data moats, distribution advantages, regulatory barriers to entry). The central argument is that the current market structure is inherently unstable: as inference costs decline along predictable experience curves and open-source models approach frontier performance, the infrastructure layer's pricing power will erode, forcing a strategic pivot toward proprietary data, vertical integration, and distribution control-a pattern with direct structural parallels to the cloud computing industry's evolution from infrastructure commodity to platform ecosystem. The paper concludes with implications for corporate strategists positioning within the AI value chain, venture capital investors evaluating AI startups, and technology policy analysts assessing market concentration risks.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p><p>The rapidly evolving market for artificial-intelligence services is apparently thriving and very competitive, with a growing number of AI start-ups and ever larger and more capable AI models. Investors are pouring large amounts of money into start-ups as well as into a few big tech firms that have large financial resources and computing capacity that constitute key inputs into the production and running of AI-driven services. Exponentially growing AI model training costs create a market entry barrier for AI start-ups, forcing them to cooperate with big tech firms to get access to computing infrastructure and end users. At the same time, their AI models compete with those of the big tech firms. Competition authorities investigate these <i>co-opetition</i> agreements, looking for market-distorting clauses. Beyond computing costs, other competition choke points in the AI supply chain include access to dedicated AI processor chips and training data. Strict enforcement of copyright on data may further tighten an already scarce supply of affordable training data.</p><p>Policymakers have few, if any, effective tools to deal with these potential competition bottlenecks in AI industries. Co-opetition agreements are necessary to enable AI start-ups to access hyperscale and costly computing infrastructure. At the same time, the agreements give &nbsp;big tech privileged access to the latest AI models. Competition authorities can try to minimise market-distorting provisions in these agreements but there are technical and economic limits to the extent of fragmentation in the AI value chain that can be meaningfully imposed on big tech firms. Licensing fees for copyright-protected data further tighten the already scarce supply of affordable data. It is hard to implement a fair market-clearing mechanism for dedicated AI processors.</p><p>If model training costs continue to grow exponentially, as appears to be the case for the foreseeable future, the entire competition policy setting for AI industries may need a revision, with collaboration, including between big tech firms, dominating competition to keep the pace of AI innovation going.</p></jats:p>

This gap between low prices and relatively limited usage share suggests that buyers value dimensions beyond price, such as quality, reliability, capabilities, ecosystem, or other forms of non-price differentiation. B Reineking. Debunking the artificial intelligence oligopoly myth: how disruption and competition shape the modern foundation model market. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt provides qualitative evidence that open-source and open-weight AI models can alter the economics of AI relative to closed, proprietary models, but it does not supply the requested quantitative comparisons of usage shares, market shares, cost or price differences, consumer-surplus estimates, or the specific findings of Nagle and Yue. It distinguishes fully open-source models—whose code, architecture, weights, training data or documentation, and training process are publicly available—from open-weight models, which make trained weights available for downloading and local or cloud use but generally impose license restrictions. Economically, open models can reduce dependence on commercial providers by allowing applications to avoid API fees and service requirements. They also support unrestricted fine-tuning for specialized tasks, potentially lowering application-development costs and encouraging innovation and entry, although using them generally requires greater technical expertise. The excerpt indicates substantial ecosystem adoption: DeepSeek R1 reportedly exceeded 700,000 downloads from Hugging Face in April 2025, while the cited notes report more than 1.75 million open models hosted there by May 2025. Closed-model applications remain important through vertically integrated products and APIs, but open models provide an alternative layer of competition and transparency. The excerpt indicates that funding affects not only how much academia engages with AI, but also the degree of control researchers retain over the models. Both public and private funding are associated with greater AI engagement. Public funding is linked particularly to broad, off-the-shelf use and open-weight models, whereas private funding is associated more strongly with extending models through fine-tuning or building on them. Industry cloud credits are specifically associated with closed models, and industry involvement is linked to model extension, potentially through coauthorship and corporate resources. Across fields and country groups, off-the-shelf AI use is increasing. The major international divide is therefore less about whether AI is adopted than about dependence on proprietary infrastructure and control over models. The Global South has seen API-only engagement rise from 0.4% to 10.0% of engaged papers, indicating greater reliance on externally hosted, potentially closed models. China presents the opposite pattern, with the highest public-funding share and the lowest API-only engagement. Public-funding shares are declining across the Global North. Overall, capacity indicators suggest convergence in AI adoption, while dependence on proprietary systems diverges. The study analyzes 104,226 papers published from 2018–2025 and characterizes engagement as model extension, off-the-shelf use, or peripheral reference.

Consequently, open models can remain practically inaccessible to researchers lacking capital, compute, and engineering capacity, leaving users dependent on commercial APIs or expensive local deployments. {"answer": "## The Economic and Scientific Impact of Open-Weight and Open-Source AI Models Compared with Closed Models

### 1. Usage Shares and Market Structure

Despite substantial cost advantages, open-source AI models account for a minority of inference market usage. Analysis of the LLM inference API market shows that open-source models represent less than 30% of market share on average, even though they are approximately 87% cheaper than comparable closed-source models conditional on model intelligence (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). This gap suggests that buyers value dimensions beyond price—including capability, reliability, ecosystem integration, and support. Nevertheless, the open-weight ecosystem has grown rapidly: by May 2025, more than 1.75 million open models were hosted on Hugging Face, and DeepSeek R1 alone exceeded 700,000 downloads from that platform in April 2025 (pqac-00000001).

According to Epoch AI data reported in the Stanford AI Index 2025, the most common release mechanism for notable AI models in 2024 was API access (32.8%), followed by open weights with restricted use (18.03%), unreleased models (16.39%), unrestricted open weights (11.48%), noncommercial open weights (9.84%), and hosted access without an API (8.20%) (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000042). Thus, "open versus closed" is best understood as a spectrum rather than a binary.

### 2. Cost and Price Differences

The cost advantage of open models has been documented across multiple settings. In the inference API market, open-source models are estimated to be 87% cheaper than closed-source models at comparable intelligence levels (pqac-00000002). Production case studies show even larger savings: replacing GPT-4 with self-hosted open-source small language models (SLMs) yielded cost reductions of 5× to 29× in a real product deployment (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045). In a laboratory-scale evaluation, fine-tuned open-weight model inference cost $0.31 versus $2.65 for GPT-4-Turbo—an approximately 88% reduction—with competitive or superior quality after domain adaptation (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

The broader trend in LLM inference pricing has been dramatic. Economy-tier models exhibit a price half-life of approximately 1.10 years—substantially faster than Moore's Law—while mid-tier models have a 1.55-year half-life (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). GPT-3-level input pricing fell from $60 per million tokens in June 2020 to approximately $0.10 per million tokens for economy models by early 2025, a roughly 600-fold nominal reduction (pqac-00000028). Quality-adjusted frontier costs have fallen approximately 5–10× per year, with algorithmic efficiency gains (after adjusting for hardware improvements) contributing roughly 3× per year for open-weight models (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Open-source model prices change more frequently (10.5% of usage-weighted provider-model-week observations) compared to closed-source models (0.9%), reflecting more intense provider-level competition (pqac-00000035).

### 3. Consumer Surplus and the Latent Role of Open Models

Nagle and Yue (2025), in their paper "The Latent Role of Open Models in the AI Economy," examine the broader economic role of open models in the AI ecosystem. While this paper was identified by multiple sources and cited in the literature (pqac-00000000), its full text was not obtainable for direct analysis. The broader evidence base suggests that open models generate substantial but partially hidden economic value. Analogous to the open-source software ecosystem—which is estimated to generate over $8 trillion in value and appears in 96% of commercial software (pqac-00000003)—open AI models likely create significant consumer surplus through lower prices, expanded access, greater customization, and competitive pressure on closed providers. The finding that open models are ~87% cheaper yet hold less than 30% of market share implies that the competitive discipline they impose benefits even users of closed models (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

### 4. Stock Market Evidence on Value Redistribution

Event-study evidence from 39 major LLM releases (November 2022–July 2026) reveals that open-weight and closed model releases redistribute value across the AI value chain in opposite directions. Open-weight releases generated a software-minus-compute spread of +2.20% (software firms: +1.28%, compute firms: −0.91%), while closed releases produced a spread of −2.30% (software firms: −2.11%, compute firms: +0.18%). The 4.5-percentage-point difference between open and closed releases was statistically significant (Welch t = 2.98; permutation p = 0.004) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). This suggests that open weights reduce expected rents associated with scarce upstream compute infrastructure while expanding opportunities for downstream software and application providers.

### 5. Innovation and Diffusion Effects

Open-weight models function as important engines of innovation and technology diffusion. Structurally, openness reduces downstream fine-tuning costs, enables self-hosting and local deployment, and broadens participation in adaptation and experimentation (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). A structural model of foundation-model openness estimated that short-term benefits of openness account for less than half of its contemporaneous costs, implying that longer-term considerations—particularly knowledge spillovers from downstream developers that improve future model generations—are the primary rationale for open strategies (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Empirically, for-profit organizations are 14–18% less likely to open-source models, but Big Tech firms are approximately 20% more likely than other for-profit organizations to do so, reflecting strategic ecosystem considerations (pqac-00000005).

In science, the diffusion of open models has been particularly pronounced. Since 2019, 92% of adopted foundation models in scientific papers were open-weight, and open models were customized 42% of the time versus only 23% for closed models (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000055). Foundation-model use in scientific publications reached 1.4% of all publications by 2024, with especially rapid growth in chemistry and biology (pqac-00000050). Open models enable researchers to download, adapt, and deploy models locally, supporting reproducibility and domain-specific innovation (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

### 6. Performance Convergence

The performance gap between open-weight and closed models has narrowed dramatically. On the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the leading closed-weight model's advantage over the leading open-weight model declined from 8.0% in January 2024 to 1.7% by February 2025. On MMLU, the gap fell from 15.9 points in late 2023 to just 0.1 point at the end of 2024, driven largely by Meta's Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek V3 (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000043). This convergence strengthens the competitive pressure that open models exert across the market.

### 7. Risk Assessments: The 2024 NTIA Report

The 2024 NTIA report on dual-use foundation models with widely available model weights adopted a conditional, risk-based approach rather than recommending a blanket prohibition on open weights (pqac-00000039). NTIA identified substantial benefits of open availability, including strengthening cyber deterrence and defense, supporting safety research and vulnerability discovery, and enabling transparency and accountability through independent third-party audits (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039). At the same time, the report identified corresponding risks: widely available models could reduce barriers for nonexperts seeking to develop chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons; facilitate offensive cyber operations; and enable disinformation at scale (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039).

Academic assessments have emphasized the concept of *marginal risk*—the additional risk attributable to open models beyond what is already possible with closed models or pre-existing technologies. Kapoor et al. (2024) concluded that existing research is "insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies" (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Bommasani et al. (2024), writing in *Science*, found that for disinformation, dissemination and platform control are more important bottlenecks than content generation; for biosecurity, comparable information is already publicly available; and for cybersecurity, open code models could strengthen defensive capabilities alongside any offensive potential (pqac-00000018). Open-weight models present a larger attack surface because safeguards can be removed and distribution is irreversible, but the evidence base for quantifying incremental harm remains limited (pqac-00000021).

### 8. Trends in Model Openness by Sector and Country

**By sector:** Industry has become the dominant producer of notable AI models. According to Epoch AI data reported in the Stanford AI Index 2025, industry produced 90.2% of notable models in 2024, with industry–academia collaborations at 8.2% and industry–government collaborations at 1.64%; standalone academia or government produced no notable models in that year's accounting (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024). Google led overall with 187 notable models from 2014–2024, followed by Meta (82), Microsoft (39), and OpenAI (36). Academic institutions such as Carnegie Mellon and Stanford (25 each), Tsinghua and UC Berkeley (22 each) remained contributors but at much smaller scale (pqac-00000024).

**By country:** The United States led in 2024 with 40 notable models, followed by China with 15 and France with 3 (pqac-00000022). However, China has emerged as the dominant source of open-weight models adopted in science: by 2026, Chinese-developed model families represented 61% of open-weight selections in single-family scientific papers, with Qwen alone accounting for 83% of that share (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000053). China's research community shows the highest public-funding share and lowest API-only engagement, while the Global South exhibits a contrasting pattern—API-only engagement rose from 0.4% to 10.0% of engaged papers, indicating growing dependence on externally hosted, often closed, models (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050).

**Open science patterns:** Public funding is associated with greater open-weight model use, while private funding and industry cloud credits are associated with closed-model and API-only reliance (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). The gap across research systems is "not one of AI adoption but of control"—off-the-shelf use is rising across fields and country groups, but dependence on proprietary infrastructure is diverging (pqac-00000049).

The following table synthesizes the key quantitative and qualitative findings across all dimensions examined:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Summary

The literature reveals that open-weight AI models exert substantial competitive pressure on closed alternatives through dramatically lower costs (87% cheaper conditional on capability), rapidly narrowing performance gaps, and broad diffusion in science and industry. Open models drive innovation through knowledge spillovers, downstream adaptation, and ecosystem expansion, while creating intertemporal incentives for firms to trade short-run monetization for long-run platform growth. The inference market has experienced "super-Moore's Law" pricing declines, with economy-tier half-lives of approximately 1.1 years, driven partly by competition among open-model hosts. However, open models remain a minority of commercial usage, their production is overwhelmingly concentrated in industry rather than academia, and their geographic diffusion reflects national technology ecosystems—particularly China's growing dominance in open-weight scientific use. Risk assessments, including the 2024 NTIA report, have adopted conditional, evidence-based frameworks rather than recommending blanket restrictions, recognizing that the marginal risks of open weights over existing technologies remain empirically uncertain while the innovation, competition, and transparency benefits are substantial."}

Nevertheless, the open-weight ecosystem has grown rapidly: by May 2025, more than 1.75 million open models were hosted on Hugging Face, and DeepSeek R1 alone exceeded 700,000 downloads from that platform in April 2025 (pqac-00000001).

According to Epoch AI data reported in the Stanford AI Index 2025, the most common release mechanism for notable AI models in 2024 was API access (32.8%), followed by open weights with restricted use (18.03%), unreleased models (16.39%), unrestricted open weights (11.48%), noncommercial open weights (9.84%), and hosted access without an API (8.20%) (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000042). Thus, "open versus closed" is best understood as a spectrum rather than a binary.

### 2. Cost and Price Differences

The cost advantage of open models has been documented across multiple settings. In the inference API market, open-source models are estimated to be 87% cheaper than closed-source models at comparable intelligence levels (pqac-00000002). Production case studies show even larger savings: replacing GPT-4 with self-hosted open-source small language models (SLMs) yielded cost reductions of 5× to 29× in a real product deployment (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045). In a laboratory-scale evaluation, fine-tuned open-weight model inference cost $0.31 versus $2.65 for GPT-4-Turbo—an approximately 88% reduction—with competitive or superior quality after domain adaptation (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

The broader trend in LLM inference pricing has been dramatic. Economy-tier models exhibit a price half-life of approximately 1.10 years—substantially faster than Moore's Law—while mid-tier models have a 1.55-year half-life (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). GPT-3-level input pricing fell from $60 per million tokens in June 2020 to approximately $0.10 per million tokens for economy models by early 2025, a roughly 600-fold nominal reduction (pqac-00000028). Quality-adjusted frontier costs have fallen approximately 5–10× per year, with algorithmic efficiency gains (after adjusting for hardware improvements) contributing roughly 3× per year for open-weight models (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Open-source model prices change more frequently (10.5% of usage-weighted provider-model-week observations) compared to closed-source models (0.9%), reflecting more intense provider-level competition (pqac-00000035).

### 3. Consumer Surplus and the Latent Role of Open Models

Nagle and Yue (2025), in their paper "The Latent Role of Open Models in the AI Economy," examine the broader economic role of open models in the AI ecosystem. While this paper was identified by multiple sources and cited in the literature (pqac-00000000), its full text was not obtainable for direct analysis. The broader evidence base suggests that open models generate substantial but partially hidden economic value. Analogous to the open-source software ecosystem—which is estimated to generate over $8 trillion in value and appears in 96% of commercial software (pqac-00000003)—open AI models likely create significant consumer surplus through lower prices, expanded access, greater customization, and competitive pressure on closed providers. The finding that open models are ~87% cheaper yet hold less than 30% of market share implies that the competitive discipline they impose benefits even users of closed models (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

### 4. Stock Market Evidence on Value Redistribution

Event-study evidence from 39 major LLM releases (November 2022–July 2026) reveals that open-weight and closed model releases redistribute value across the AI value chain in opposite directions. Open-weight releases generated a software-minus-compute spread of +2.20% (software firms: +1.28%, compute firms: −0.91%), while closed releases produced a spread of −2.30% (software firms: −2.11%, compute firms: +0.18%). The 4.5-percentage-point difference between open and closed releases was statistically significant (Welch t = 2.98; permutation p = 0.004) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). Open-weight models function as important engines of innovation and technology diffusion. Structurally, openness reduces downstream fine-tuning costs, enables self-hosting and local deployment, and broadens participation in adaptation and experimentation (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). A structural model of foundation-model openness estimated that short-term benefits of openness account for less than half of its contemporaneous costs, implying that longer-term considerations—particularly knowledge spillovers from downstream developers that improve future model generations—are the primary rationale for open strategies (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Foundation-model use in scientific publications reached 1.4% of all publications by 2024, with especially rapid growth in chemistry and biology (pqac-00000050). The performance gap between open-weight and closed models has narrowed dramatically. This convergence strengthens the competitive pressure that open models exert across the market.

The 2024 NTIA report on dual-use foundation models with widely available model weights adopted a conditional, risk-based approach rather than recommending a blanket prohibition on open weights (pqac-00000039). (2024) concluded that existing research is "insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies" (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). (2024), writing in *Science*, found that for disinformation, dissemination and platform control are more important bottlenecks than content generation; for biosecurity, comparable information is already publicly available; and for cybersecurity, open code models could strengthen defensive capabilities alongside any offensive potential (pqac-00000018). ## The Economic and Scientific Impact of Open-Weight and Open-Source AI Models Compared with Closed Models

### 1. Usage Shares and Market Structure

Despite substantial cost advantages, open-source AI models account for a minority of inference market usage. Analysis of the LLM inference API market shows that open-source models represent less than 30% of market share on average, even though they are approximately 87% cheaper than comparable closed-source models conditional on model intelligence (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). This gap suggests that buyers value dimensions beyond price—including capability, reliability, ecosystem integration, and support. Nevertheless, the open-weight ecosystem has grown rapidly: by May 2025, more than 1.75 million open models were hosted on Hugging Face, and DeepSeek R1 alone exceeded 700,000 downloads from that platform in April 2025 (pqac-00000001).

According to Epoch AI data reported in the Stanford AI Index 2025, the most common release mechanism for notable AI models in 2024 was API access (32.8%), followed by open weights with restricted use (18.03%), unreleased models (16.39%), unrestricted open weights (11.48%), noncommercial open weights (9.84%), and hosted access without an API (8.20%) (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000042). Thus, "open versus closed" is best understood as a spectrum rather than a binary.

### 2. Cost and Price Differences

The cost advantage of open models has been documented across multiple settings. In the inference API market, open-source models are estimated to be 87% cheaper than closed-source models at comparable intelligence levels (pqac-00000002). Production case studies show even larger savings: replacing GPT-4 with self-hosted open-source small language models (SLMs) yielded cost reductions of 5× to 29× in a real product deployment (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045). In a laboratory-scale evaluation, fine-tuned open-weight model inference cost $0.31 versus $2.65 for GPT-4-Turbo—an approximately 88% reduction—with competitive or superior quality after domain adaptation (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

The broader trend in LLM inference pricing has been dramatic. Economy-tier models exhibit a price half-life of approximately 1.10 years—substantially faster than Moore's Law—while mid-tier models have a 1.55-year half-life (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034). GPT-3-level input pricing fell from $60 per million tokens in June 2020 to approximately $0.10 per million tokens for economy models by early 2025, a roughly 600-fold nominal reduction (pqac-00000028). Quality-adjusted frontier costs have fallen approximately 5–10× per year, with algorithmic efficiency gains (after adjusting for hardware improvements) contributing roughly 3× per year for open-weight models (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Open-source model prices change more frequently (10.5% of usage-weighted provider-model-week observations) compared to closed-source models (0.9%), reflecting more intense provider-level competition (pqac-00000035).

### 3. Consumer Surplus and the Latent Role of Open Models

Nagle and Yue (2025), in their paper "The Latent Role of Open Models in the AI Economy," examine the broader economic role of open models in the AI ecosystem. While this paper was identified by multiple sources and cited in the literature (pqac-00000000), its full text was not obtainable for direct analysis. The broader evidence base suggests that open models generate substantial but partially hidden economic value. Analogous to the open-source software ecosystem—which is estimated to generate over $8 trillion in value and appears in 96% of commercial software (pqac-00000003)—open AI models likely create significant consumer surplus through lower prices, expanded access, greater customization, and competitive pressure on closed providers. The finding that open models are ~87% cheaper yet hold less than 30% of market share implies that the competitive discipline they impose benefits even users of closed models (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).

### 4. Stock Market Evidence on Value Redistribution

Event-study evidence from 39 major LLM releases (November 2022–July 2026) reveals that open-weight and closed model releases redistribute value across the AI value chain in opposite directions. Open-weight releases generated a software-minus-compute spread of +2.20% (software firms: +1.28%, compute firms: −0.91%), while closed releases produced a spread of −2.30% (software firms: −2.11%, compute firms: +0.18%). The 4.5-percentage-point difference between open and closed releases was statistically significant (Welch t = 2.98; permutation p = 0.004) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). This suggests that open weights reduce expected rents associated with scarce upstream compute infrastructure while expanding opportunities for downstream software and application providers.

### 5. Innovation and Diffusion Effects

Open-weight models function as important engines of innovation and technology diffusion. Structurally, openness reduces downstream fine-tuning costs, enables self-hosting and local deployment, and broadens participation in adaptation and experimentation (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). A structural model of foundation-model openness estimated that short-term benefits of openness account for less than half of its contemporaneous costs, implying that longer-term considerations—particularly knowledge spillovers from downstream developers that improve future model generations—are the primary rationale for open strategies (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Empirically, for-profit organizations are 14–18% less likely to open-source models, but Big Tech firms are approximately 20% more likely than other for-profit organizations to do so, reflecting strategic ecosystem considerations (pqac-00000005).

In science, the diffusion of open models has been particularly pronounced. Since 2019, 92% of adopted foundation models in scientific papers were open-weight, and open models were customized 42% of the time versus only 23% for closed models (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000055). Foundation-model use in scientific publications reached 1.4% of all publications by 2024, with especially rapid growth in chemistry and biology (pqac-00000050). Open models enable researchers to download, adapt, and deploy models locally, supporting reproducibility and domain-specific innovation (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000011).

### 6. Performance Convergence

The performance gap between open-weight and closed models has narrowed dramatically. On the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the leading closed-weight model's advantage over the leading open-weight model declined from 8.0% in January 2024 to 1.7% by February 2025. On MMLU, the gap fell from 15.9 points in late 2023 to just 0.1 point at the end of 2024, driven largely by Meta's Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek V3 (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000043). This convergence strengthens the competitive pressure that open models exert across the market.

### 7. Risk Assessments: The 2024 NTIA Report

The 2024 NTIA report on dual-use foundation models with widely available model weights adopted a conditional, risk-based approach rather than recommending a blanket prohibition on open weights (pqac-00000039). NTIA identified substantial benefits of open availability, including strengthening cyber deterrence and defense, supporting safety research and vulnerability discovery, and enabling transparency and accountability through independent third-party audits (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039). At the same time, the report identified corresponding risks: widely available models could reduce barriers for nonexperts seeking to develop chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons; facilitate offensive cyber operations; and enable disinformation at scale (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000039).

Academic assessments have emphasized the concept of *marginal risk*—the additional risk attributable to open models beyond what is already possible with closed models or pre-existing technologies. Kapoor et al. (2024) concluded that existing research is "insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies" (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). Bommasani et al. (2024), writing in *Science*, found that for disinformation, dissemination and platform control are more important bottlenecks than content generation; for biosecurity, comparable information is already publicly available; and for cybersecurity, open code models could strengthen defensive capabilities alongside any offensive potential (pqac-00000018). Open-weight models present a larger attack surface because safeguards can be removed and distribution is irreversible, but the evidence base for quantifying incremental harm remains limited (pqac-00000021).

### 8. Trends in Model Openness by Sector and Country

**By sector:** Industry has become the dominant producer of notable AI models. According to Epoch AI data reported in the Stanford AI Index 2025, industry produced 90.2% of notable models in 2024, with industry–academia collaborations at 8.2% and industry–government collaborations at 1.64%; standalone academia or government produced no notable models in that year's accounting (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024). Google led overall with 187 notable models from 2014–2024, followed by Meta (82), Microsoft (39), and OpenAI (36). Academic institutions such as Carnegie Mellon and Stanford (25 each), Tsinghua and UC Berkeley (22 each) remained contributors but at much smaller scale (pqac-00000024).

**By country:** The United States led in 2024 with 40 notable models, followed by China with 15 and France with 3 (pqac-00000022). However, China has emerged as the dominant source of open-weight models adopted in science: by 2026, Chinese-developed model families represented 61% of open-weight selections in single-family scientific papers, with Qwen alone accounting for 83% of that share (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000053). China's research community shows the highest public-funding share and lowest API-only engagement, while the Global South exhibits a contrasting pattern—API-only engagement rose from 0.4% to 10.0% of engaged papers, indicating growing dependence on externally hosted, often closed, models (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050).

**Open science patterns:** Public funding is associated with greater open-weight model use, while private funding and industry cloud credits are associated with closed-model and API-only reliance (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). The gap across research systems is "not one of AI adoption but of control"—off-the-shelf use is rising across fields and country groups, but dependence on proprietary infrastructure is diverging (pqac-00000049).

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a theoretical account of how openness affects competition and welfare in the AI foundation-model value chain, but it does not supply the empirical evidence requested in the question. It does not distinguish systematically between open-weight and open-source models, report usage shares or market shares, quantify cost or price differences, estimate consumer surplus numerically, or discuss Nagle and Yue’s findings. Its central result is that openness has contingent economic effects because it interacts with licensing prices, downstream fine-tuning investment, and an incumbent’s data-flywheel advantage. The incumbent may choose maximum openness with a high price to harvest short-term profits, high openness with a low price to dominate and accelerate learning, or restricted openness to defend against future competition. The paper identifies an “openness trap”: forcing a dominant incumbent to be fully open can induce high licensing prices, reduce deployer fine-tuning, and lower consumer surplus and social welfare. It also argues that openness mandates, vertical integration, and subsidies can redistribute surplus among developers, deployers, entrants, and end users, with outcomes depending on market conditions. Thus, the excerpt supports a nuanced claim that openness is not automatically pro-competitive or welfare-enhancing, while leaving the requested quantitative comparisons and Nagle–Yue evidence unaddressed.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that open-source models exert strong price competition relative to closed models. Weekly prices changed in 10.5% of open-source provider-model-token observations, versus only 0.9% for closed-source models. Open-source pricing is therefore more flexible and generally lower, while closed providers maintain relatively rigid prices across model generations. Prices also vary substantially among models with similar intelligence—by up to two orders of magnitude—and closed-source models tend to command a premium over comparable open models. contexts.context: The excerpt provides an economic framework for comparing open and closed AI models, but it does not report the specific usage shares, market shares, cost or price differences, consumer-surplus estimates, or Nagle and Yue findings requested in the question. Its central claim is that open sourcing creates a trade-off: it may accelerate model improvement, software growth, complementary innovation, and R&D through external contributions, while closed models can generate immediate revenue through API sales or licensing. Empirically, a model with a larger performance advantage over the leading open-source model is less likely to be released openly: a 10-point quality lead is associated with a 10–11 percentage-point reduction in open-sourcing likelihood. For-profit organizations are on average 14–18% less likely to open source, whereas Big Tech firms are estimated to be 20% more likely than other for-profit organizations to do so. The paper also finds that LLMs are compatible with the R&D portfolios of many technologically diverse firms, suggesting broad economic applicability, and reports increased research-related activity after Meta open sourced LLaMA. The theoretical model predicts an inverted-U relationship between firm size and open-sourcing propensity: moderate ownership of compatible applications favors openness, while very small firms prioritize immediate revenue and firms with dominant internal resources may gain less from community contributions.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames open-source and open-weight foundation models as producing two simultaneous effects on innovation and diffusion. First, openness increases knowledge spillovers: future entrants can learn from the incumbent’s technology, which lowers barriers to entry and intensifies longer-run competition. This can broaden experimentation and support innovation beyond the original model developer. Second, openness reduces downstream fine-tuning costs, encouraging deployers to invest in adapting models for specialized applications. Lower adaptation costs can accelerate adoption, stimulate ecosystem growth, and diffuse foundation-model capabilities across products and domains. The excerpt also describes a data flywheel: downstream use generates user feedback, prompt adjustments, contextual data, and tacit expertise that improve application performance and reduce future fine-tuning costs. Thus, open models can speed initial diffusion and downstream innovation, while repeated use creates cumulative learning. However, the effects are not uniformly positive. Greater openness can empower rivals through spillovers, while the incumbent may benefit from stronger downstream engagement and learning-based lock-in. The broader paper therefore treats openness as a strategic trade-off rather than an unambiguously beneficial policy: its impact on competition, investment, welfare, and diffusion depends on the balance between knowledge transfer to entrants and reduced downstream adaptation costs.
contexts.question: What are the innovation and diffusion effects of open-source and open-weight AI foundation models? How do open models affect scientific research, downstream innovation, knowledge spillovers, and technology diffusion?

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes open foundation models as mechanisms that broaden technology diffusion by making model weights widely available, lowering barriers for downstream users, and enabling local deployment. Greater access, customization, and local inference expand the range of applications and support more aggressive adaptation, including fine-tuning, quantization, and pruning. Local adaptation allows developers to work with proprietary or sensitive datasets without transferring them to a model provider, which can facilitate innovation in privacy-sensitive domains. Open models may also advance research and technical capabilities across languages and applications, while access to model checkpoints and related assets has enabled substantial downstream scientific work. Their broader availability distributes the ability to define acceptable model behavior among more downstream developers rather than leaving it solely to a foundation-model provider, potentially increasing diversity in applications and approaches. However, model weights alone are insufficient for important scientific investigations: studying bias propagation, validating evaluations, and detecting benchmark contamination often requires training data and other artifacts. Thus, openness can produce knowledge spillovers and innovation, but the research benefits depend on the availability of complementary assets and transparency. The excerpt also notes potential tradeoffs: local or otherwise unobserved inference makes monitoring and moderation difficult, and open models can be customized to remove alignment interventions.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents open-source and open-weight foundation models as mechanisms that trade some upstream control and immediate monetization for broader innovation and diffusion. Making model weights available enables downstream developers to download, self-host, fine-tune, adapt, and deploy models independently, separating the model from any single infrastructure provider and allowing distribution through cloud platforms, specialized inference providers, and public repositories. This lowers dependence on the original model owner and supports wider technology diffusion, although meaningful use still requires computing resources, engineering, maintenance, and security capabilities. Open models also broaden participation in innovation: experimentation, customization, collaborative development, and knowledge creation are distributed across firms, individual developers, and competitors. Downstream adoption can generate feedback about failure modes, safety vulnerabilities, desired capabilities, data needs, and deployment constraints that were not identified internally. Public derivative models, adapters, evaluation results, bug reports, and related artifacts can therefore produce knowledge spillovers and contribute to later model improvement. The excerpt also emphasizes an intertemporal ecosystem effect: openness may expand downstream adoption and future ecosystem rents, improving subsequent foundation-model quality even when it reduces direct access-based revenue. Hugging Face provides an observable, though incomplete, window into these downstream innovation activities.

Openness reduces barriers for downstream developers to fine-tune, evaluate, deploy, and build applications on existing models. These activities generate indirect contributions—fine-tuning data, usage patterns, bug reports, performance feedback, and application experience—that produce knowledge spillovers. The model owner can incorporate this ecosystem-generated knowledge into later model generations, so the main innovation effect is intertemporal: openness of the current release can improve the quality and competitiveness of future models rather than merely modifying the current one. This creates a feedback loop in which higher-quality models attract more developers, expanding adoption and generating further experimentation, evaluation, and knowledge. The framework therefore links diffusion to both downstream innovation and future model improvement, while also potentially expanding market share and ecosystem rents. The excerpt does not directly measure effects on scientific research, nor does it specifically distinguish open-source from open-weight models; its empirical focus is on foundation-model openness, downstream adoption and activity, and subsequent model quality. It also cautions that the reported relationships are conditional and descriptive rather than definitive causal effects, because model-specific investment and demand shocks may remain. contexts.context: The excerpt presents open-weight models as enabling important forms of diffusion and downstream innovation, especially because downloadable parameters support local execution, preservation, and adaptation while reducing dependence on unilateral API changes. However, openness does not automatically produce transparent or reproducible science: training data and development procedures may remain unavailable, model behavior is difficult to explain, and technical reproducibility does not ensure replication. The study finds that the scientific diffusion of open-weight AI is geographically and institutionally structured rather than evenly global. In 2026, Chinese-developed models represented 61% of open-weight selections in single-family papers, with 83% attributable to Qwen. Chinese institutions were substantially more likely to use Chinese model families, while the same pattern did not extend to non-Chinese open-weight models. Thus, open models can generate global knowledge and technology spillovers, but adoption remains embedded in language, geography, professional networks, and domestic technology ecosystems. The excerpt characterizes this as a redistribution of scientific dependence—from proprietary systems such as GPT toward ecosystems including Qwen and DeepSeek—rather than its disappearance. Innovation and diffusion therefore depend not simply on openness, but on the performance, price, accessibility, institutional support, and geopolitical ecosystem surrounding particular models.

Because open models can be downloaded and applied or customized by anyone, they are overwhelmingly represented among scientific adoptions: 92% of adopted models across fields since 2019 were open. Finally, open models remain dominant despite closed-model adoption growing faster: from 2020 to 2023, closed-model usage grew 336% annually versus 20% for open models.
